food.text: During the Ming dynasty, China joined the Columbian Exchange, a new global trade in goods, plants, animals and food crops. Although most imports were silver, the Chinese also bought New World crops from the Spanish Empire, including sweet potatoes, maize and peanuts.

Chili peppers were first mentioned in Hunan's local gazettes in 1684, the 21st year of the Kangxi Emperor. Today Hunan cuisine is famous for its hot and spicy flavours, though only about 20% of it uses capsicum to make a strong spicy taste.

Qing imperial cuisine was built on the traditional diet of the Manchu ethnic group and Shandong cuisine. The famous Manchu Han Imperial Feast was created during this dynasty, and its meal rites and sumptuous courses were the greatest of any dynasty in China.
Sweet potatoes, maize and peanuts could grow in lands where wheat, millet and rice could not. This helped facilitate a rise in the population of China.

The Qing imperial palace had a special Imperial Kitchen, managed by the General Office of Internal Affairs. During the reign of the Qianlong Emperor (1735 to 1796), it was divided into an Internal Kitchen and an External Kitchen that prepared palace banquets, feasts and sacrificial rites.

Century eggs are known to have been part of Chinese cuisine since at least the 17th century. Their transforming agent is an alkaline salt, which gradually raises the egg's pH to around 9 to 12. This chemical process breaks down complex proteins and fats into smaller flavorful compounds.
In the Song dynasty, rice had become the major staple crop of the poor. After sweet potatoes were introduced to China around 1560, they gradually became the traditional food of the lower classes.

The Portuguese were allowed to settle in Macau in 1557 for trade. After the Spanish invasion of the Philippines, trade with the Spanish at Manila brought large quantities of Mexican and Peruvian silver into China.

Hunan cuisine is known as gan la, meaning 'dry and spicy' or purely hot, with liberal use of chili peppers, shallots and garlic. This contrasts with Sichuan cuisine, whose ma la seasoning is 'numbing and spicy' and uses Sichuan pepper along with chilies.

Ming dynasty writers produced books on food and health, such as Chen Jiru's Gentlemen's Remark on Diets and Liu Ruoyu's History of the Ming Palace - Preferences for Diets. Diet therapy for good health was an important part of imperial cuisine.

The 17th-century writer Fang Yizhi described how preserved eggs were made in his book Little Knowledge of Physics. He wrote that eggs from Chizhou were salted with five kinds of tree ash. Buckwheat grain ash gave them a yellow and white look, and charcoal lime made them green and tough.

In the Ming dynasty, the need for more food pushed prices up, and more of the lower class citizens died as a result. This followed the spread of New World crops such as sweet potatoes, which became the traditional food of the lower classes after being introduced to China around 1560.

art.text: Wen Zhengming (1470-1559) developed the style of the Wu school in Suzhou. That style dominated Chinese painting during the 16th century.
Early Qing painting developed in two strands, the Orthodox school and the Individualist painters. Both followed the theories of Dong Qichang, but they emphasized very different aspects of them.

Famille rose porcelain was introduced late in the reign of the Kangxi Emperor (1661-1722), possibly around 1720. It used mainly pink or purple and allowed a greater range of colour and tone than before, enabling more complex images. It stayed popular through the 18th and 19th centuries and was widely adopted by European factories.
Dong Qichang (1555-1636) absorbed ideas from Chan Buddhism and put forward the "Southern and Northern Schools" theory. Through it he influenced East Asian art history well beyond China.

Jieziyuan Huazhuan, the Manual of the Mustard Seed Garden, was first published in 1679 as a five-volume work. Made possible as color printing techniques were perfected, it has been used as a technical textbook for artists and students ever since.
tags: Manual of the Mustard Seed Garden

art.text: The mud-brick Emin Minaret in Turpan is 44 metres tall, making it the tallest minaret in China. It was started in 1777 during the reign of the Qianlong Emperor and completed only one year later, and its exterior is decorated with sixteen patterns of textured bricks.

The Four Wangs, including Wang Jian (1598-1677) and Wang Shimin (1592-1680), were renowned in the Orthodox school. They sought inspiration in recreating past styles, especially the brushstrokes and calligraphy skills of ancient masters.

The Individualist painters Bada Shanren (1626-1705) and Shitao (1641-1707) drew on ideas of transcending tradition to reach original styles. In this way they followed the way of Dong Qichang more faithfully than the Orthodox school, who were his official direct followers.

The Jesuit missionary Père François Xavier d'Entrecolles lived in Jingdezhen in the early 18th century. In a letter dated 1712 he described how pottery stones were crushed, refined and formed into little white bricks known as petuntse, in the hope that the details might be useful in Europe.

The younger Wang Yuanqi (1642-1715) ritualized the approach of drawing inspiration from a work by an ancient master. He often annotated his own paintings with his theories of how they related to the master's model.

Historians note that Chinese painting had a deep and far-reaching impact on Tibetan visual art during the 18th century. Giuseppe Tucci said that by the time of the Qing dynasty a new Tibetan art had developed, which he called a provincial echo of the Chinese 18th century's smooth ornate preciosity.

war.text: In 1521 and again in 1522, the Ming navy repulsed the Portuguese at Tuen Mun. European traders who reached China during the Age of Discovery were repeatedly rebuked in their requests for trade. The Portuguese were allowed to settle in Macau in 1557.

During the rule of the Jiajing Emperor (1507–1567), wokou piracy ravaged the southeastern coastline of China, and raids by the Pisheye from Taiwan and the Philippines also ravaged the southern coasts. Domestic and foreign demand for overseas trade, which the state deemed illegal, fueled the piracy. It only subsided after ports in Guangdong and Fujian were opened and after much military suppression.
The Dutch entry into the Chinese seas was met with fierce resistance. In the Sino-Dutch conflicts of 1622–1624, the Dutch were chased off the Penghu islands and forced to settle in Taiwan instead.
The Dutch in Taiwan fought the Ming at the Battle of Liaoluo Bay in 1633 and lost. They eventually surrendered to the Ming loyalist Koxinga in 1662, after the fall of the Ming dynasty.

China had no unified navy, and individual provinces managed naval defenses. After the Qianlong Emperor died in 1799, the navy decayed as attention turned to suppressing the Miao Rebellion and White Lotus Rebellion. These conflicts left the Qing treasury bankrupt.

literature.text: During the Ming and Qing dynasties, mature novels were written in written vernacular Chinese. This was an evolution away from the preeminence of Literary Chinese, which was patterned off the language of the Chinese classics.

Writing classical Chinese poetry became a conventional skill of the well-educated throughout the Ming and Qing dynasties. Over a million poems have been preserved from these centuries, including many by women and by other voices.

The scholar Jonathan Chaves urged that the sheer quantity of Ming poetry, the quality of so much of it, and its stylistic richness and diversity all cry out for serious attention. This was said even though China's late imperial period is not known for innovative approaches to poetry.
Several painter-poets of the Ming and Qing era combined art, poetry and calligraphy with brush on paper. They included Shen Zhou, Tang Yin, Wen Zhengming and Yun Shouping (1633 to 1690).

The Ming-Qing transition was a difficult time for poets, with the late Ming ruled by the Chongzhen Emperor, then the short-lived regime of the peasant rebel Li Zicheng, and then the Manchu Qing. Poets who wrote through it include the so-called Three Masters of Jiangdong: Wu Weiye, Qian Qianyi and Gong Dingzi.

The Complete Tang Poems anthology, compiled in the early eighteenth century under the Qing, includes over 48,900 poems written by over 2,200 authors. It preserved the poetry of the Tang dynasty for later readers.

China had no counterpart to the 19th-century European explosion of novels. The earlier Ming and early Qing novels remained well known to most Chinese, either directly or through adaptations to Chinese opera and other forms of popular culture.
Among the many poets of the Ming and Qing era were women such as Dong Xiaowan and Liu Rushi. Their work is part of the more than a million poems preserved from those dynasties.
Poetry composition competitions were socially common in Ming and Qing China. Writing verse was a shared social activity as well as a private art.

Three Hundred Tang Poems, a Qing dynasty selection, has made Tang poetry familiar to educated Chinese in modern times. Many poems in it have been adopted by Chinese textbooks and are regarded as must-recite ones.

The Classic of Poetry stresses female authorship, since many songs appear to be written by women or from a female perspective. This emphasis was made much of when women poets of the Ming-Qing period sought canonical status for their own poems.

Since the Qing dynasty, the rhyme patterns of the Classic of Poetry have been analysed in the study of Old Chinese phonology. The ancient anthology of 305 works became a source for linguistic research as well as literature.

science.text: The Kangxi Emperor of the Qing dynasty decided that Chinese maps were not accurate enough and needed scientific methods. He sponsored a nationwide mapping programme based on astronomical observation and triangulation measurements. The resulting map, begun in 1708, took over 10 years to complete.

In the 16th century, China adopted the European compass-card, with its box frame and dry pivot needle, via Japanese pirates. Even so, the older Chinese suspended dry compass persisted well into the 18th century. That design used a turtle-shaped wooden frame holding a lodestone sealed in wax.

Historian Joseph Needham spent decades documenting Chinese science and technology. His research led him to ask why modern science stopped developing in China after the 16th century. His question became a famous puzzle in the history of science.

In the late Ming dynasty, traditional Chinese mapmaking became more developed and advanced. This happened under the influence of new ideas of technology and studies of natural science that were introduced from the West to China.

Needham believed the answer lay in China's sociopolitical system. China did not have a structure in which merchants could profit from their inventions, unlike the West. He argued that gunpowder, the compass, paper and printing helped transform European feudalism into capitalism.
The Huang Yu Quan Lan Tu, also known as the Jesuit Atlas, was the first on-the-spot survey map in Chinese cartography. It had 41 framings based on provincial boundaries.

Not all Ming maps aimed at scientific precision. Yu Shi's Gujin xingsheng zhi tu (1555) and Zhang Huang's Tushu bian (1613) use no gridlines. Instead, illustrations and annotations show mythical places, exotic foreign peoples, administrative changes and the deeds of historic and legendary heroes.

The idea of the Four Great Inventions came from the West, not China. Reports by Portuguese sailors and Spanish missionaries began reaching Europe in the 1530s, and Europeans learned that these inventions had existed in China for centuries. By 1620, Francis Bacon wrote that printing, gunpowder and the nautical compass had altered the face and state of the world.

Some scholars argue that Chinese technological superiority before the 16th century shows Chinese science was crucial to modern science's foundation. American sinologist Nathan Sivin counters that, before the scientific revolution, technology was not a good measure of scientific capacity.

politics.text: In 1636, Hong Taiji renamed his state from "Great Jin" to "Great Qing" and raised his title from Khan to Emperor. He did so after receiving the imperial seal of the Yuan dynasty, a move that suggested imperial ambitions beyond unifying the Manchu territories.

The Qing seized the Ming capital Beijing and North China in 1644, traditionally counted as the start of the dynasty's rule. At its height the Qing controlled more territory than any dynasty in Chinese history.

The Ming dynasty became increasingly isolationist after the Yongle Emperor died. The treasure voyages across the Indian Ocean were discontinued, and maritime prohibition laws banned the Chinese from sailing abroad.

Overseas trade that the Ming state deemed illegal fueled widespread wokou piracy attacking the southeastern coastline during the reign of the Jiajing Emperor. Raids from Japan by the wokou, and from Taiwan and the Philippines by the Pisheye, ravaged the southern coasts. The raids only subsided after ports in Guangdong and Fujian were opened and much military suppression was carried out.
The Ming navy repulsed the Portuguese at Tuen Mun in 1521 and again in 1522. Yet in 1557 the Portuguese were allowed to settle in Macau for trade, and it remained in Portuguese hands until 1999.

Genghisid rulers retreated to the Mongolian Plateau after the Ming defeated the Yuan in 1368. They kept ruling as the Northern Yuan until 1635, when they surrendered to the Later Jin, which later evolved into the Qing dynasty.

Within a few decades of taking power, the Qing began calling their expansive empire both the Great Qing and, nearly interchangeably, China. Instead of the earlier Ming idea of an ethnic Han Chinese state, this new Qing China was a self-consciously multi-ethnic state.

The Dutch were chased off the Penghu islands in the Sino-Dutch conflicts of 1622 to 1624 and forced to settle in Taiwan. They lost the Battle of Liaoluo Bay to the Ming in 1633, and in 1662 surrendered to the Ming loyalist Koxinga.

In 1634 Hong Taiji created his own artillery corps after the Jurchens suffered defeat in 1627, partly due to the Ming's newly acquired Portuguese cannons. His gunsmiths cast cannons in the European design with the help of defector Chinese metallurgists.

The Qianlong Emperor commissioned the Illustrated Precedents for the Ritual Paraphernalia of the Imperial Court by 1759, and it was published and enforced by 1766. It set dress codes for the imperial family and officials, aiming to preserve Manchu identity while aligning the emperor's image with Confucian ideas.

In 1616, the Jurchen chieftain Nurhaci declared himself a khan and founded the Later Jin dynasty. His successors renamed it the Qing dynasty in 1636, the same year Hong Taiji introduced the name "Manchu" for the Jurchen people.

philosophy.text: During the 17th and 18th centuries, Catholic missionaries in China argued bitterly over whether Confucianism and Chinese rituals were religious. The dispute, known as the Chinese Rites controversy, turned on whether ancestor veneration and other formal rites were compatible with Catholic belief.

During the Ming dynasty, a resurgent Neo-Confucianism led by thinkers such as Wang Yangming (1472–1529) became the dominant school of thought. The imperial state promoted it. The same revival also took hold in Korea's Joseon dynasty.

According to Chinese Hui followers of the Qadiriyya Sufi school, Afaq Khoja gave his blessing in 1672 in Xining to the sixteen-year-old Qi Jingyi, later known as Hilal al-Din, who went on to introduce the Qadiriyya order into China. Two of his other students, Ma Laichi and Ma Mingxin, later founded the Khufiyya and Jahriyya brotherhoods after studying in Central Asia and Arabia.

The Jesuits argued that Chinese rites were secular rituals compatible with Christianity within certain limits, and so should be tolerated. The Dominicans and Franciscans disagreed and reported the issue to Rome.

In the 16th century, Jesuit missions to China began to play a significant role in the emerging dialogue between China and the West. The Jesuits adapted Chinese religious ideas, such as admiration for Confucius and ancestor veneration, into the doctrine they taught in China.

By the end of the seventeenth century the Jesuits had made many converts. They were impressed by the knowledge and intelligence of the Han Chinese Confucian scholar elite, and adapted to their ancient Chinese intellectual lifestyle.

Rome's Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith first sided with the Dominicans in 1645, condemning the Chinese rites. In 1656 it sided with the Jesuits and lifted the ban. The judgment on Chinese rituals thus reversed within eleven years.
tags: Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith

philosophy.text: Pope Clement XI condemned the Chinese rites and Confucian rituals in 1704 with the decree Cum Deus optimus, issued on 20 November. He also outlawed any further discussion of the matter.

The Jesuit Matteo Ricci began a tradition in the 16th century of using Shangdi as the Chinese name for the Christian God. The term derives from the Shang theology of the high god Di, and is sometimes also used for the Jade Emperor of Taoism.

In 1724 the Yongzheng Emperor proscribed the Heavenly Lord sect, the name given to Catholicism at that time. Persecution steadily increased during his reign. Although he admired the Jesuit Giuseppe Castiglione's artwork, he reinforced anti-Christian policies in 1737.

culture.text: The Yixing region of China gave rise to the first true teapot in the 16th century. Monks from the Jinsha Temple, also called the Golden Sand Temple, began making unglazed teapots from the local clay near Yixing.

Under the Qing dynasty, many different types of tea rose in popularity. By the mid-18th century, white, black and oolong teas were well known and being sold internationally, having become a major cash crop for China.

Four novels, Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Water Margin, Journey to the West, and The Golden Lotus, are seen as a technical breakthrough reflecting new cultural values. Their authors used ironic narratives that carried a Neo-Confucian moral critique of late Ming decadence.
Yixing purple clay (zisha) was porous and retained heat well. Because it absorbed the taste of tea over time, a process known as seasoning, it affected the flavor of any tea later brewed in the pot.
The Story of the Stone, or Dream of the Red Chamber, circulated in manuscript until it was edited and printed in 1791. It is widely considered the greatest of the traditional Chinese novels.

The use of the new teapots was popularized by Gong Chun, who became a servant in the house of Yixing tea master Wu Lun (1440 to 1522). Simplicity and rusticity dominated the idea of purple clay teawares, which soon became quite popular.
The Qing court promoted milk tea, a traditional Manchu drink. It also popularized scented teas, including jasmine tea and teas scented with cloranthus, cassia, honeysuckle, and rose.
The Quantangshi, or Complete Tang Poems, was compiled in the early eighteenth century. This anthology includes over 48,900 poems written by over 2,200 authors.
The gastronome Yuan Mei (1716 to 1797) wrote about 18th century Wuyi mountain oolongs in Recipes from the Garden of Contentment. He also described the local tea customs of his day.
tags: Recipes from the Garden of Contentment
